## Today

You walk out with a topic, a set of search terms that actually work, and the start of a
search log. That log is most of the Librarian Visit Report.

**No librarian is coming to us.** You book your own appointment at Lovejoy and go to them,
and that meeting is the assignment. Today is how you arrive there with something worth
their time.

**Have a topic in mind.** Rough is fine.

## Thirty sources in an hour

- You find one article that looks right. It cites twelve others.
- You chase three of those. Each cites fifteen more.
- An hour later you have thirty sources open and no idea which one to read first
- The instinct is to retreat: narrow the topic, keep three recent articles, hope
- That instinct is completely reasonable, and following it is what makes the next
  three weeks harder than they need to be

## It is a map, not a reading list

A **literature review** is not evidence that you read enough articles. It is a map of who
has said what, and where the arguments are.

Think of it as walking into a debate that has been running for years. Say your piece cold
and you get told it was answered in 2012. Knowing the terrain is how you earn the right to
ask your question.

You cannot map terrain from three landmarks, which is why retreating to three articles
fails.

## What a review does for you

- **It shows where your work sits.** You are not the first person to wonder this.
- **It finds the gap**, which is your answer to "so what?"
- **It stops you rebuilding something that already exists.** Your original idea may be
  somebody's dissertation from five years ago.
- **It hands you methods**: measures that have been validated, sampling strategies, and
  other people's documented limitations (Krippendorff, 2018; Neuendorf, 2017)
- **It sharpens the question** from "something about Twitch chat" into something you can
  actually answer

## Your turn {.discuss}

- Name a media topic you are curious about, in one sentence
- What words would a scholar use for it that you would not?
- Where would you look first, and how would you know if you had missed the main body of work?

*Two minutes to get your terms down. Your librarian will ask you for them, so this is not a
warm-up exercise.*

## Phase one: search broadly

- Start wide. You are answering basic questions, not finding your final sources.
- What words do scholars use for this? Who keeps coming up? Which journals publish it?
- **Google Scholar** first. Less thorough than the real databases, and fast and free.
- **Wikipedia** is not citable, and its reference list is still a doorway
- Collect anything promising in **Zotero** and tag freely. Do not tidy yet.

## Phase two: search systematically

Now you want coverage rather than speed, which means the real databases:

- **Communication & Mass Media Complete**, the main one for our field
- **PsycINFO** if your question touches emotion, persuasion, or cognition
- **Web of Science** and **Scopus** for tracking citations across disciplines

These do not work like Google. They expect **Boolean operators**, which is the next slide.

## Building a search string

**AND** narrows, so both terms must appear. **OR** widens. **NOT** excludes. An asterisk is
a wildcard: `stream*` catches stream, streams, streaming, and streamer.

```
(livestream* OR "live streaming" OR Twitch) AND
(motivation* OR gratification* OR engagement) AND
(viewer* OR audience* OR chat)
```

Three concept blocks joined with AND, each holding its own synonyms. Build yours the same
way and take it with you: a librarian can fix a string like this in seconds.

## Keep a search log

Plain text, in your repository. For every search you run, write down:

- The date and which database
- The exact string, copied and pasted, never remembered
- The limiters you set and how many results came back
- How many you kept

**You should see** it getting boring to write, which is the point. It lets you defend the
strategy later, and it shows you fast which searches are not working.

## Phase three: follow the citations

- Pick a few **keystone articles**, the ones that clearly sit at the centre
- **Backward chaining:** read what they cite, which takes you to the foundations
- **Forward chaining:** use Google Scholar's "Cited by" to see who has cited them since,
  which shows you how the argument moved
- It snowballs, but on purpose, following the network out from what matters most rather
  than wandering

## Knowing when to stop

**Saturation** is the point where more searching stops changing your understanding. You
will recognise it three ways:

- Three database searches in a row turn up nothing new that is relevant
- New articles keep citing the same eight or ten sources you have already read
- You can guess what an article says from its title and abstract

It does not mean you read everything. It means stop searching and start synthesizing.

## Book your librarian appointment

[Do this today, not Thursday]{.eyebrow}

- Go to [Lovejoy Library](https://www.siue.edu/lovejoy-library/) and ask for the
  **Mass Communications subject librarian** by name. That is what they are there for.
- Book it **this week**. The report is due Friday and their calendar is not yours.
- Bring your topic, your terms, and your search log. A consultation with nothing in hand
  wastes the half hour and gives you nothing to write up.
- This is the part a chapter cannot give you: the interface, the limiters, and the tricks
  that only come from using these every day.

## What to ask while you are there

- Which database is actually right for **my** question?
- How do I get the full text when the library does not subscribe?
- How do I set up a saved search and an alert for new results?
- What is the fastest way to push a batch of results into Zotero?
- Interlibrary loan is free and much faster than you expect. Ask how to use it.

## The rest of today: search, in here, now

- Open a database and run your first real string. I am walking the room.
- Start the search log on your **first** search, not once you have something good
- Before you leave: a topic, one string that works, and three sources in Zotero
- Bring me the search that returns 40,000 hits, or the one that returns none. Both are
  normal and both are fixable in about a minute.

## Last part of today: commit your work

You have a topic, a working string, and the start of a search log. None of it is anywhere
but your laptop.

Download this into the **top folder** of your workspace, beside `README.md`:

[aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/starters/01-commit-your-work.qmd](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/starters/01-commit-your-work.qmd)

**Getting that file onto GitHub is the check.** It is not in the template, so if I can see it
in your repository, you put it there yourself.

## Save, stage, commit, push

1. **Save** it, `Ctrl+S`. The dot in the tab turns back into an X.
2. **Source Control** in the left bar, or `Ctrl+Shift+G`. Your file is listed with a **U**.
3. **Stage** it: hover over the name, click the **+**. It moves to Staged Changes.
4. Type a **message** a stranger could read, then click **Commit**. Never "update".
5. Click **Sync Changes**. The first time from a folder it says **Publish Branch** instead.

**You should see** the file on your repository page at github.com when you refresh it. A
commit stays on your laptop; the push is what sends it. You need both, every time.
